title: Ethics, the broker's day job & how the market talks
recap: The CII Code of Ethics boils down to: follow the rules, act with integrity, put the client first, give good service, treat people fairly, and stay competent through CPD.
Conflicts of interest must be identified, then prevented or managed; disclosure is the last resort, not a free pass.
Every client is told how the broker is paid before cover starts; commercial clients can ask for the commission amount, and consumers must be told any fee up front.
Demands and needs apply to every sale, suitability applies whenever you recommend, and if it isn't written down, it didn't happen.
A broker's week mixes renewals, new business, claims advocacy, underwriter relationships, and admin and compliance.

sections.heading: Professionalism: what the Code of Ethics asks of you
sections.body:
As a dietitian you're registered with the HCPC and work to its standards. Broking has a similar idea. Most brokers belong to the **Chartered Insurance Institute (CII)**, the professional body for insurance, and members sign up to its **Code of Ethics**. It isn't law in the way FCA rules are, but breaching it can lead to CII disciplinary action, up to losing membership.

Stripped of formal language, the Code asks you to:

- **Follow the law and the rules**, including the FCA's rules and the CII's own.
- **Act with integrity**: be honest, don't mislead, and never let a sale matter more than the truth.
- **Act in your client's best interests**: their needs come before your commission or your sales target.
- **Give a good standard of service**: do what you said you'd do, when you said you'd do it.
- **Treat people fairly**, whoever they are.

### Competence and CPD

You'll recognise the next bit. You should only do work you're competent to do, and you have to keep that competence current. That's **CPD** (continuing professional development): courses, webinars, reading and technical updates, logged as you go. Under the FCA's insurance distribution rules, people involved in selling insurance must complete at least 15 hours a year, and CII members have their own CPD requirement too. Exams like IF1 are usually where that journey starts.

The FCA backs all this up. Its Principles expect every firm to act with integrity and with due skill, care and diligence, and the Consumer Duty requires good outcomes for retail customers. Ethics in broking isn't a poster on the wall; it's built into the regulation.

sections.heading: Conflicts of interest and being open about money
sections.body:
A **conflict of interest** is any situation where what's good for you or your firm could pull against what's good for your client. They're everywhere in broking, and having one isn't wrong in itself. Failing to spot and handle it is.

Some everyday examples:

- Insurer A pays 20% commission and insurer B pays 12%, but B is the better fit for the client.
- Your firm earns a bonus if it places a certain volume of business with one insurer.
- Your firm holds a binder (authority to underwrite on an insurer's behalf), so on that business you're partly wearing the insurer's hat.
- Two clients are chasing the same limited insurer capacity in a tight market.

FCA rules expect firms to **identify** conflicts, then **prevent or manage** them (clear policies, separate teams, recommending on merit and recording why). Only where managing isn't enough to protect the client do they **disclose** the conflict, clearly and before the client commits. Disclosure is the last resort, not a free pass.

### Being open about money

Brokers are paid by **commission** (a percentage of the premium, paid by the insurer), by a **fee** charged directly to the client, or a mix of both. Before a policy is arranged, every client must be told the *nature* of the broker's pay: fee, commission or both.

- **Commercial customers** can ask how much commission the broker is earning, and the broker must tell them promptly.
- **Consumers** must be told the amount of any fee before they're committed, so it's never a surprise on the invoice.

Beyond the specific rules there's a general expectation of transparency. The Consumer Duty's *price and value* outcome means a retail product, broker's earnings included, has to be fair value. A good test: if the client saw exactly what you earned and why, would you be comfortable?

sections.heading: Demands & needs, suitability and writing it down
sections.body:
Before any insurance is arranged, the broker must work out what the customer needs and wants (their **demands and needs**) and make sure the policy offered is consistent with them. This applies to every sale, advised or not. It's written up in a **demands and needs statement** for the customer: here's what you told us, here's what you need, here's how this policy meets it, and where it doesn't.

Think of it as the insurance version of a pre-assessment. You wouldn't write a care plan before taking a history.

### Advised versus non-advised

If a broker makes a **personal recommendation** ("this is the one I'd choose for you"), it must be **suitable**: right for the client's needs and circumstances, with the reasons explained. In a non-advised sale the broker still checks demands and needs and gives clear information, but leaves the choice to the client. Most commercial and health broking is advised.

Suitability includes pointing out what *isn't* covered. Flagging that a PMI policy excludes pre-existing conditions, or that a liability limit looks low for the client's contracts, is part of the job.

### If it isn't written down, it didn't happen

You already live by this one. Clinical notes protect the patient (continuity and safety) and protect you (if a complaint lands, the record shows what you did and why). Broking files work exactly the same way.

A good file shows what the client told you, the questions you asked, which insurers you approached and what they said, what you recommended and why, what the client chose, and any warnings you gave. If a client later says "nobody told me flood wasn't covered", your meeting note is your evidence. Without it, a complaints handler or the Financial Ombudsman Service may well conclude it was never said.

Records protect the client too. When a claim arrives two years later, the file shows exactly what was disclosed to the insurer, which helps the broker argue the client's case.

sections.heading: A broker's week
sections.body:
There's no single typical day, but most brokers juggle the same five strands. In health and employee benefits broking the rhythm is the same; the risks are people rather than buildings.

### Renewals

Most policies run for a year, so much of the job is a rolling **renewal cycle**. For a commercial client, work often starts around three months out: update the client's information, gather claims experience, go to the current insurer (and often others), negotiate, then present options with a recommendation in time for the client to decide. Popular dates such as 1 January and 1 April create busy peaks. Miss a renewal and the client could be left uninsured, a classic source of complaints.

### New business

Brokers also need to grow. That means prospecting (networking, referrals, events, LinkedIn), meeting potential clients, understanding their business and preparing a proposal. Winning a client often involves a letter of appointment so the new broker can approach insurers for them.

### Claims advocacy

When something goes wrong, the broker is the client's champion: helping notify the claim, gathering evidence, explaining the cover and pushing the insurer for a fair, prompt outcome. In health broking that might be chasing a PMI pre-authorisation for an employee's surgery. This is where clients decide whether you're worth it.

### Market relationships

Brokers spend real time with **underwriters**, the people at insurers who decide whether to take a risk and on what terms. Knowing which insurer wants what, and having a relationship that gets your call returned on a Friday afternoon, is genuine value for clients.

### Admin and compliance

Then the unglamorous bit: updating the client system, checking documents are accurate, writing file notes, chasing premiums, compliance file reviews and CPD logs. It feels like paperwork. It's also what keeps clients protected and the firm out of trouble.

sections.heading: Glossary: 49 terms you'll hear in a broking office
sections.body:
Here are the words you'll hear in your first week, in plain English. Don't try to memorise them all at once; come back to this list after each module.

- **TOBA** — Terms of Business Agreement: the contract setting out how a broker and an insurer (or client) work together.
- **Slip** — The London-market document summarising a risk, which underwriters sign to take a share.
- **Binder** — A binding authority letting an intermediary accept risks for an insurer within agreed rules.
- **MGA** — Managing General Agent: a firm authorised by insurers to underwrite on their behalf.
- **Bordereau** — A regular report to the insurer of policies written or claims paid under delegated authority.
- **Rate** — The price per unit of exposure, such as per £100 insured or a percentage of wage roll.
- **Loss ratio** — Claims divided by premium, shown as a percentage.
- **Run-off** — Business no longer written but with past claims still to settle, or cover for those claims after a firm stops trading.
- **Premium** — The price the client pays for the insurance.
- **Excess** — The amount the policyholder pays first on each claim.
- **Deductible** — Similar to an excess, usually a larger amount a business carries itself.
- **Limit** — The most the insurer will pay, per claim or in total.
- **Aggregate** — A limit capping the total of all claims in the period, not each claim.
- **Endorsement** — A formal change to the policy wording or schedule.
- **Schedule** — The personalised page showing who is insured, sums insured, period and premium.
- **Wording** — The full policy terms, conditions and exclusions.
- **Cover note** — Temporary proof of cover before the full documents are issued.
- **Quote** — An insurer's offer of terms and price, valid for a limited time.
- **Renewal** — Continuing cover for another period, usually a year.
- **Lapse** — When a policy ends because it isn't renewed or the premium isn't paid.
- **Mid-term adjustment (MTA)** — A change during the policy period, often with extra or returned premium.
- **Claims-made** — Cover triggered by claims first made during the policy period, common in professional indemnity.
- **Losses-occurring** — Cover triggered by losses happening during the period, whenever claimed.
- **Retroactive date** — On a claims-made policy, the date before which incidents are not covered.
- **IPT (Insurance Premium Tax)** — A tax on most general insurance premiums, including PMI (standard rate 12%).
- **Commission / brokerage** — The broker's pay from the insurer as a percentage of premium.
- **Fee** — A charge the broker makes directly to the client.
- **Net vs gross premium** — Gross includes the broker's commission; net is what the insurer keeps after it.
- **Underwriter** — The person at an insurer who decides whether to accept a risk and on what terms.
- **Placing** — Finding insurers to take a risk and getting cover agreed.
- **Market** — The insurers you can approach, or one of them.
- **Capacity** — How much risk an insurer can or will take on.
- **Appetite** — The kinds of risk an insurer actively wants to write.
- **Facility** — A pre-arranged deal with insurers to place a type of business on agreed terms.
- **Delegated authority** — Any arrangement letting a third party underwrite or handle claims for an insurer.
- **Cedant / reinsurer** — The cedant passes (cedes) part of its risk; the reinsurer takes it on.
- **Excess of loss** — Cover, often reinsurance, paying above an agreed amount up to a limit.
- **Subjectivity** — A condition the quote or cover depends on, such as a satisfactory survey.
- **Declaration** — A client statement confirming facts or reporting figures such as actual wage roll.
- **Long-term agreement (LTA)** — A deal to stay with one insurer for, say, two or three years for stable rates.
- **Claims experience / loss runs** — The client's claims history over several years, used for pricing.
- **Broker of record (BOR) letter** — A client's letter appointing a broker to act for them, often replacing another.
- **Open market vs scheme** — Open market places each risk individually; a scheme is a pre-agreed package for similar clients.
- **Wholesale** — A broker placing business for other brokers, not end clients.
- **Retail** — A broker that deals directly with the client.
- **PMI** — Private medical insurance, which pays for private treatment of acute conditions.
- **Group risk** — Employer-paid group life, income protection and critical illness cover.
- **Employee benefits (EB)** — What employers offer beyond salary, such as pension, PMI and group risk.
- **Wellbeing** — Services keeping staff healthy, such as virtual GP and mental health support.

whyItMatters: Clients rarely judge a broker on the policy wording; they judge them on honesty, how well they listened and whether they fought their corner at claim time. Knowing the vocabulary means you can follow the conversation from day one instead of nodding along.

questions.stem: Under the CII Code of Ethics, whose interests should a broker put first when recommending a policy?
options: The firm's, since it carries the regulatory risk
The insurer's, since it pays the commission
The client's, by acting in their best interests
Whichever party is paying the broker on that deal
questions.explanation: Acting in each client's best interests is a core duty of the Code, so the client's needs come before commission, targets or insurer relationships. Who pays the broker doesn't change who the broker works for.

questions.stem: What does CPD mean for an insurance broker?
options: Ongoing learning, logged each year, to keep knowledge and skills up to date
A one-off qualification that permanently proves competence
A disciplinary process for brokers who breach the Code of Ethics
The annual review of client files carried out by compliance
questions.explanation: Continuing professional development is ongoing, recorded learning, much like CPD for HCPC registration. Passing an exam starts the journey but doesn't replace keeping up to date.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes a conflict of interest in broking?
options: A disagreement between a broker and an underwriter over price
A client complaint that has been escalated to the Ombudsman
Two insurers offering identical terms on the same risk
A situation where the broker's own interests could pull against the client's
questions.explanation: A conflict exists whenever the broker or firm stands to gain from something that may not be best for the client, such as higher commission. A price negotiation with an underwriter is normal business, not a conflict.

questions.stem: When a firm identifies a conflict of interest, what does the FCA expect it to do?
options: Disclose it to the client and then carry on as normal
Prevent or manage it, and disclose it clearly if managing it isn't enough to protect the client
Take no action unless the client raises it
Refuse to act for the client in every case
questions.explanation: Disclosure is the last resort, not a free pass: the firm must first try to prevent or manage the conflict. Many conflicts can be managed, so refusing to act is not automatically required.

questions.stem: What is a demands and needs statement?
options: The insurer's list of the risks it is willing to write
The client's signed declaration that their information is true
A document recording what the customer needs and how the proposed policy meets them
The schedule showing sums insured and premium
questions.explanation: It sets out what the customer told the broker, what they need, and how (and where not) the policy matches. The insurer's list of preferred risks is its appetite, a different thing.

questions.stem: When must a broker make sure a recommendation is 'suitable' in the regulatory sense?
options: Whenever they give the client a personal recommendation
Only when the client is a consumer rather than a business
Only when arranging health or life cover
Only when the premium is above a set amount
questions.explanation: Suitability is triggered by advice: once a broker says "this is right for you", it must fit the client's needs and the reasons must be explained. It applies to business clients as well as consumers.

questions.stem: In a broking office, what is a 'TOBA'?
options: A temporary document proving cover before the policy is issued
A report of claims paid under a binding authority
A client's letter appointing a new broker
A Terms of Business Agreement setting out how a broker and an insurer (or client) work together
questions.explanation: A TOBA sets the ground rules of the relationship, such as responsibilities and who holds premium money. A temporary proof of cover is a cover note.

questions.stem: An MGA sends its insurer a monthly spreadsheet listing every policy written and the premium collected. What is this called?
options: A slip
A bordereau
A cover note
A loss run
questions.explanation: A bordereau is the regular report sent to an insurer about business written or claims paid under delegated authority. A loss run is one client's claims history.

questions.stem: In a broking office, what is an MGA?
options: A government body that supervises insurers' capital
A broker that only deals with other brokers
A firm given authority by insurers to underwrite business on their behalf
A group of insurers sharing a single large risk
questions.explanation: A Managing General Agent underwrites under delegated authority from one or more insurers. A broker that only deals with other brokers is a wholesale broker.

questions.stem: A client paid £100,000 in premium and their claims cost £65,000. What is the client's loss ratio?
questions.explanation: Loss ratio is claims divided by premium: £65,000 ÷ £100,000 = 65%. Dividing the other way round gives the 154% figure, a common slip.

questions.stem: On a claims-made policy, what does the retroactive date do?
options: Sets the last date a claim can be notified after the policy ends
Marks the date the premium is due
Fixes the date from which a higher excess applies
Excludes incidents that happened before that date
questions.explanation: Claims-made cover responds to claims made in the period, but only for incidents on or after the retroactive date. Keeping that date unchanged when switching insurers avoids gaps in cover.

questions.stem: Halfway through the policy year, a client adds a second van to their commercial vehicle policy. What is this change called?
options: A renewal
A mid-term adjustment
A lapse
A subjectivity
questions.explanation: A mid-term adjustment (MTA) is any change during the policy period, often with an extra or returned premium. A renewal happens only at the end of the period.

questions.stem: An insurer's quote says 'subject to a satisfactory fire risk survey within 30 days'. What is this condition called?
options: An endorsement
A declaration
A subjectivity
An aggregate
questions.explanation: A subjectivity is a condition the quote or cover depends on being met. An endorsement is a formal change to an existing policy's wording or schedule.

questions.stem: What is a wholesale broker?
options: A broker that places business for other brokers rather than dealing with end clients
A broker that only arranges large corporate policies
An insurer that sells directly to the public
A broker that only works on schemes
questions.explanation: Wholesale brokers give retail brokers access to specialist or London markets. Size of client has nothing to do with it; a retail broker can handle very large corporates.

questions.stem: What is the difference between gross and net premium?
options: Gross includes the excess; net excludes it
Gross is the annual premium; net is the monthly instalment
Gross is before claims are paid; net is after
Gross includes the broker's commission; net is what the insurer keeps after commission
questions.explanation: Gross premium is the full premium including the broker's commission; net is what's left for the insurer once commission is deducted. The excess is part of the claim, not the premium.

questions.stem: Two insurers offer Poppy's friend's café similar cover. Insurer A pays the broker 20% commission; Insurer B pays 12% but has better business interruption cover for the café. What should the broker do?
options: Recommend Insurer A, since the premiums are similar
Recommend Insurer B on its merits and record the reasons
Present both without comment and let the owner pick
Ask Insurer B to match Insurer A's commission before recommending anything
questions.explanation: The client's best interests come first, so the better-fitting cover wins and the file shows why. Staying silent when the broker has been asked for advice ducks the duty to recommend suitably.

questions.stem: The owner of a small building firm asks her broker exactly how much commission they're earning on her liability policy. What must the broker do?
options: Decline, because commission is commercially confidential
Tell her only if the commission is above 20%
Tell her the amount promptly, because commercial customers are entitled to ask
Refer her to the insurer, who sets the commission
questions.explanation: A commercial customer can ask for the amount of commission and the broker must disclose it promptly. There's no threshold, and the broker can't pass the question to the insurer.

questions.stem: Poppy's brother uses a broker for his home insurance, and the broker charges an arrangement fee on top of the premium. When should he be told the amount of the fee?
options: Before he commits to the policy
When the invoice arrives
Only if he asks
At the first renewal
questions.explanation: Consumers must be told the amount of any fee before they are committed, so they can factor it into the decision. Telling him afterwards defeats the point.

questions.stem: A client complains that their broker never warned them flood damage was excluded. The broker remembers mentioning it at the meeting but made no note. Why is the broker in a weak position?
options: Because flood exclusions are not allowed on commercial policies
Because the insurer is always liable for the broker's spoken comments
Because brokers may not discuss exclusions verbally
Because without a record, a complaints handler may conclude the warning was never given
questions.explanation: Just like clinical notes, if it isn't written down it's hard to prove it happened. A short file note of the warning would have been the broker's best evidence.

questions.stem: A commercial client's policy renews on 1 April. When would a broker typically start work on the renewal?
options: The week before, once the insurer sends renewal terms
Around three months before, gathering updated information and claims experience
On 1 April, so the information is as current as possible
After the policy lapses, so the client can compare prices freely
questions.explanation: Starting early gives time to update information, test the market and let the client decide before cover runs out. Leaving it late risks a gap in cover, a classic complaint.

questions.stem: An employee on her company's PMI scheme is struggling to get pre-authorisation for knee surgery, and HR asks the broker for help. What is the broker's role?
options: To stay out of it, because claims are purely between the insurer and the employee
To decide the claim themselves, since they placed the policy
To act as advocate, explaining the cover and pressing the insurer for a fair, prompt decision
To move the scheme to another insurer immediately so the claim is paid
questions.explanation: Claims advocacy is a core part of the broker's job: they don't decide claims, but they help the client get a fair hearing. Switching insurers mid-claim wouldn't get an existing claim paid.

questions.stem: An accountant's professional indemnity policy is claims-made and runs for the calendar year. In March, a client makes a claim about advice given three years ago. The retroactive date is five years ago. Which policy responds?
options: This year's policy, because the claim is first made now and the advice post-dates the retroactive date
The policy that was in force three years ago, when the advice was given
Neither, because claims-made policies only cover advice given in the current year
Next year's policy, once the claim is settled
questions.explanation: Claims-made cover is triggered by when the claim is made, not when the advice was given, as long as the incident falls after the retroactive date. The old-year answer describes a losses-occurring basis.

questions.stem: A firm's product liability policy has a £2 million aggregate limit. It has already paid two claims totalling £1.8 million this year. A third claim for £500,000 arrives. What is the most the policy can pay towards it?
options: £500,000, because each claim has its own limit
£2 million, because the limit resets after each claim
Nothing, because two claims have already been paid
£200,000, the amount left in the aggregate
questions.explanation: An aggregate limit caps the total of all claims in the period, so only £200,000 remains. A per-claim ("any one claim") limit would have allowed the full £500,000.

questions.stem: A broker has a pre-agreed package with set rates and wording for dental practices, and a new dentist client fits it neatly. What is this kind of arrangement called?
options: An open-market placement
A scheme
A long-term agreement
An excess of loss treaty
questions.explanation: A scheme is a ready-made arrangement for a group of similar clients. Open market means approaching insurers individually for that one client.

questions.stem: Which statement about demands and needs is true?
options: It only applies when the broker gives advice
It only applies to consumers, not businesses
It applies to every sale, and the policy offered must be consistent with the customer's needs
It can be completed after the policy starts, at the first renewal
questions.explanation: Demands and needs is required on all sales, advised or not, consumer or commercial, before the contract is concluded. Suitability is the extra layer that applies when advice is given.

questions.stem: Which statement about broker remuneration is true?
options: Clients must be told the nature of the broker's pay (fee, commission or both) before the policy is arranged
Commission is banned on commercial insurance
Consumers have no right to know whether a fee is charged
A broker who charges a fee must not also receive commission
questions.explanation: Every client is told how the broker is paid before cover is arranged. Commission is perfectly legal, and many brokers combine fees and commission as long as both are disclosed.

questions.stem: Which statement is true?
options: The excess is the most the insurer will pay on a claim
The limit is the amount the policyholder pays first on each claim
An endorsement is the page showing the policyholder's name, sums insured and premium
The schedule is the personalised part of the policy showing the client's details, sums insured and premium
questions.explanation: The schedule personalises the policy; an endorsement changes it. The excess and limit are easily swapped: the excess is what the client pays first, the limit is the most the insurer pays.

questions.stem: Which statement about delegated authority is true?
options: Only Lloyd's syndicates can grant it
It lets a third party such as a broker or MGA accept risks on an insurer's behalf within agreed rules
It means the broker carries the insurance risk itself
It removes the insurer's responsibility for paying claims
questions.explanation: Under delegated authority the insurer still carries the risk and pays claims; it simply lets someone else underwrite within set limits. Company-market insurers grant it as well as Lloyd's.

questions.stem: Which statement about the CII Code of Ethics is true?
options: It is an Act of Parliament enforced by the courts
It only applies to brokers who deal with consumers
Breaching it can lead to CII disciplinary action, including loss of membership
Following it means a firm no longer needs to follow FCA rules
questions.explanation: The Code is a professional standard for CII members, enforced by the CII rather than the courts. It sits alongside FCA regulation and expressly expects members to follow the law and the rules.

questions.stem: Which statement about a broker's working week is true?
options: Admin and compliance work, such as file notes, protects both the client and the firm
Relationships with underwriters matter little because prices are set by computers
Insurers find new clients, so brokers only handle renewals
Once a policy is placed, claims are left entirely to the insurer
questions.explanation: Good records and compliance checks are what let a broker prove what was said and fight a client's corner. Brokers also win new business, advocate on claims and rely on underwriter relationships.
